div.p: Describes the physical geometry of a detector - crystal shape, material and dimensions, dead layer, endcap/housing layers, an optional collimator - and produces a response that can be evaluated for a source at any distance and angle, not only on the detector axis in the far field as the flat-disk model assumes.
Three methods are offered under Location Support, plus a fourth for a detector imported from a Genie/ISOCS .par file:

ul.li: No MC support (instant, from measured curve): no Monte Carlo is run. The detector's measured efficiency curve is held fixed at its measurement distance and transferred to other positions by the ratio of ray-traced, attenuation-weighted solid angles (the EFFTRAN idea). This is the default, and is what a DRF made with a geometry in the "Create Detector Response Function" tool carries.
Quick MC: Monte Carlo along the detector axis only (plus a few angles), transferred elsewhere as above. A fraction of the cost of a full characterization.
Full MC: Monte Carlo over energy, angle and distance. Takes minutes, and is the choice when sources will be measured well off-axis or in contact with the detector.

Imported efficiency grid: only offered for a detector imported from a .par file, and selected by default for one. The file's efficiency grid (energy, distance and angle) is used as-is, so the geometry cannot be edited while it is selected. It is full-energy peak only: there is no total efficiency, so cascade-summing corrections are not available. Building or generating another response replaces the grid.

div.p: When the detector has measured efficiency points, a generated response is corrected to them ("grounded"), so it reproduces your calibration while adding the geometry physics between and beyond it. The Response preview shows the efficiency for several source angles at a distance you choose.

Monte-Carlo characterization is worth it when measurements are made closer than a few detector diameters, or noticeably off the detector axis; for far-field, on-axis work the instant measured-curve transfer already gives the same answer.
